22.title: Born at Talwandi, 1469
22.hook: Nanak is born to Mehta Kalu and Mata Tripta in a Punjab village now called Nankana Sahib
22.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's birth each year, usually at the full moon of Kartik in the autumn, with processions, continuous readings of the scripture, kirtan and langar; many make pilgrimage to Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Japji Sahib, Nanak's morning poem, thirty-eight stanzas to climb verse by verse. Today the stories begin, with a birth.

Punjab, 1469, in the spring, if the oldest accounts are right. Wheat fields run flat to the horizon. A mud-brick village called Talwandi sits west of the city of Lahore. The landlord is a Muslim named Rai Bular. His village accountant, who keeps the records of land and harvests, is a Hindu named Mehta Kalu. And in Kalu's house, his wife, Mata Tripta, is about to have her second child. No palace, no crowd outside. Just a family, a village, a baby.
screen: `PUNJAB, 1469.` → `A VILLAGE CALLED TALWANDI.` → `A FAMILY, A VILLAGE, A BABY.`

segments.voice: The baby was Nanak. His father was a Khatri, from a caste of traders and record-keepers: a practical man who hoped his son would earn a respectable living. His mother is remembered in Sikh tradition for her gentleness and her quiet faith in her unusual son. There was an older sister, Nanaki, and she gets her own day tomorrow. The janamsakhis, the life-stories of Guru Nanak, surround the birth with signs: a room filled with light, a midwife who said she'd never seen a child like this. Sikhs tell those stories with joy. What can be said plainly is where, and roughly when. And here's an honest wrinkle. The oldest accounts put the birth in spring, in the month of Vaisakh. But Sikhs usually celebrate it at the full moon of Kartik, in October or November, following another early tradition. Scholars still argue about the date. The celebration stays in autumn, with lights, processions and all-night singing, and nobody's faith hangs on the calendar. As for the village: Talwandi is now called Nankana Sahib, Nanak's town, and since partition it has been in Pakistan. A gurdwara stands where tradition says he was born, and Sikh pilgrims still cross the border to visit it. A boy born in a village with a Muslim landlord and a Hindu accountant. It fits, somehow, for the man who'd say there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and say, quietly, the name of the place where your life began: a town, a hospital, a house. If you don't know much about it, picture what you imagine. Then name the people who were there, or waiting, as far as you know them. Nobody there knew what your life would be. Notice how small and ordinary that beginning was, and how much has grown from it.
Talwandi. The village, now called Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born in 1469, to Mehta Kalu and Mata Tripta.
Your line: every story starts somewhere small. Even this one began in a mud-brick village. Day twenty-two, done.

23.title: The sister who saw first
23.hook: his older sister, Bebe Nanaki, is remembered as the first to recognize who her brother was
23.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bebe Nanaki as Guru Nanak's devoted older sister, often called the first to recognize him; a gurdwara in her memory stands in Sultanpur Lodhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Talwandi, the small village where Nanak was born. Every story starts somewhere small. Today, the first person who saw something in him.

A dreamy boy is worrying the grown-ups of his village. In the stories the janamsakhis tell, he gives things away. He sits silent for hours. He asks the village priest and teacher questions they can't answer. His father, Mehta Kalu, loves him and worries constantly: how will this boy ever earn a living? But one person watches him with a different kind of attention, and believes in him before there is much evidence. His big sister.
screen: `A BOY WHO WORRIES THE VILLAGE.` → `ONE PERSON BELIEVES ANYWAY.` → `FOR NANAK, HIS BIG SISTER.`

segments.voice: Her name was Nanaki. Sikhs call her Bebe Nanaki: bebe is an affectionate word for an older sister or a respected woman. Tradition says she was about five years older than Nanak. To everyone else, her brother was a puzzle. Nanaki saw it differently. Sikh tradition remembers her as the first to recognize that he wasn't lost. He was found, in a way the others couldn't see yet. Some Sikhs even call her the first Sikh, the first follower of the Guru, though she was his sister before she was anything else. And she didn't stop at believing. Nanaki married a man named Jai Ram and moved to the town of Sultanpur. When her brother was a young man, drifting and at odds with his father, she brought him there. Jai Ram helped find him work, and Nanak lived near her for years. The turning point of his life, a few days from now, happened in Sultanpur, because she made room for him. The sources say little about her own inner life, and that's worth saying. What they remember is the shape of her love: she saw him first, and she made space for what she saw.

segments.voice: Let a face come to mind: someone who believed in you early, before there was much to go on. Hear their voice, remember one thing they said, and let the gratitude come without rushing. Then say the one sentence you'd tell them now, quietly or on paper.
Bebe Nanaki. Guru Nanak's older sister, remembered as the first to recognize who her brother was, and who made room for him to become it.
Your line: someone saw you first. Somebody believed before there was proof. See you tomorrow.

24.title: The boy and the teacher
24.hook: tradition says young Nanak asked his village teacher what the letters really pointed to
24.howItsDone: Sikh children often hear this story when they begin learning Gurmukhi, and Guru Nanak's Patti, an acrostic on the alphabet in the Guru Granth Sahib, is sung in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bebe Nanaki, the sister who saw her brother first and made room for him. Today, a boy at school.

Why is the sky blue? Why do we have to go to bed? Why? A small child asks it, and then asks again, and again, until the grown-up runs out of answers and says because I said so. Somewhere along the way, right answers start to crowd that question out. The story goes that when Nanak was about seven, his father took him to the village teacher to learn his letters, so that one day he could keep accounts like his dad. The teacher wrote out the alphabet on a wooden board. And the boy asked a question that stopped the lesson.
screen: `WHY? AND WHY AGAIN.` → `SEVEN YEARS OLD, AT SCHOOL.` → `A QUESTION THAT STOPPED THE LESSON.`

segments.voice: In the janamsakhis, the village teacher, a pandha, writes the letters on a wooden writing board, a patti, and tells the boy to copy them. Nanak does. And then he asks: but what do they mean? Not what sound does this letter make. What does it point to? The teacher, used to children who just copied, doesn't know what to say. And the boy, the story goes, begins to explain: each letter can point you toward God. The first letter, toward the one who made everything. The next, toward truth. And so on, all through the alphabet, until the teacher bows to the student. Here's what makes it more than a legend. In the Guru Granth Sahib there really is a poem by Guru Nanak called Patti, the writing board. It's an acrostic: it runs through the alphabet, and each letter opens a line about God and the soul. In paraphrase, one letter begins a line about the one who created the world and is master of all. Another warns the mind that it will have to give an account of itself. Some readers think Nanak composed it as a grown man, and the janamsakhi set it back in his childhood, at the moment it seemed to belong. Either way, the question is his. Tradition also says he later learned Persian from a Muslim teacher and studied Sanskrit texts too, so he wasn't against learning. He just wouldn't stop at the surface of it. The same boy who asked what the sacred thread was for, back on day six, asked what the alphabet was for. It's the question under his whole life.

segments.voice: Pick one word you use every day without thinking: home, friend, sorry, work, love. Ask Nanak's question of it: what does this really point to? Don't rush for an answer; let the word open slowly, like the letters on the teacher's board.
Patti. The wooden writing board young Nanak learned his letters on, and the name of his alphabet poem in the Guru Granth Sahib, where each letter points toward God.
Your line: ask what it means. The letters were only the start. Day twenty-four, done.

25.title: The cobra's shade
25.hook: tradition says that as he slept in the fields a cobra spread its hood to shade his face
25.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of the cobra's shade as a sakhi of Guru Nanak's youth, and pilgrims to Nankana Sahib visit the gurdwara that tradition connects with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: patti, the writing board, and a boy who asked what the letters point to. Today, a story from the fields.
screen: `THE BOY AND THE TEACHER — ASK WHAT IT MEANS.`

segments.voice: A hot afternoon in Punjab, the kind of heat that flattens everything; even the birds go quiet. In the pastures beyond Talwandi, a teenage boy has been sent to watch the family's buffaloes. His father hopes the job will teach him some responsibility. But the boy has found a tree, lain down beneath it, and fallen asleep in the heat. The sun moves. The shade slides off his face. And then, the story says, something comes out of the grass.
screen: `A HOT AFTERNOON IN THE PASTURES.` → `THE BOY FALLS ASLEEP.` → `THE SHADE SLIDES AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the story the janamsakhis tell. A cobra slides up beside the sleeping boy, raises itself, and spreads its hood wide over his face like a small umbrella, keeping him in shade. Just then Rai Bular, the Muslim landlord of Talwandi, comes riding past. He sees the boy, the snake, the hood. He doesn't reach for a stick. He understands, the story says, that he's looking at someone the world itself is protecting. From that day Rai Bular is remembered as one of the first to honor Nanak, and he defended the boy to his worried father more than once. A gurdwara in Nankana Sahib marks the place tradition connects with the story. Is it history? The sources can't say, and it's honest to admit that. Many Sikhs treasure it as a true event. Many others, and many historians, hear it as a sakhi: a story told to show something true. And what it shows is lovely. A cobra is the most dangerous creature in the field, and here the dangerous thing becomes the shelter. Something out there, even something fierce, is looking after the boy. Sikhs speak of God as the protector who keeps the ones who remember, and the story puts that in a single picture: a hood spread wide over a sleeping face. Plenty of people have known something like it: a thing that could have gone wrong and didn't, a shelter they didn't arrange.
screen: `A HOOD, SPREAD WIDE.` · `RAI BULAR RIDES PAST.` · `HISTORY OR SAKHI? SOURCES CAN'T SAY.` · `THE DANGEROUS THING BECOMES SHELTER.` · then, large: `SOMETHING SHELTERS YOU.`

segments.voice: If you can, move into some shade: a tree, a porch, the cool side of a room, or close your eyes and picture that tree in Punjab. Let your body rest completely. Bring to mind one time you were protected without arranging it, a near miss or a stranger's help, and let yourself feel sheltered.
Sapp. The cobra that spread its hood over the sleeping Nanak to shade him, and the landlord, Rai Bular, who saw it and understood.
Your line: something shelters you. Even when you didn't arrange it, and didn't see it coming. That's day twenty-five.

26.title: The true bargain
26.hook: sent with twenty rupees to strike a good deal, he feeds hungry holy men and comes home empty-handed
26.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of sacha sauda as an early sign of the langar and of Guru Nanak's teaching on sharing; Gurdwara Sacha Sauda in Pakistan marks the place tradition connects with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sapp, the cobra that spread its hood over a sleeping boy. Something shelters you. Today, a trip to the market.

Mehta Kalu has had enough. His son is a young man now, and he still hasn't shown the slightest interest in making money. The buffaloes wandered. The lessons turned into questions. So the father tries one more thing, the thing a practical man would try. He counts out twenty rupees, a real sum, puts it in his son's hand, and says: go to the market town. Buy something you can sell for more. Make a good deal. Bring back a profit. The son nods, takes the money, and sets off down the road. He does make a deal. Just not the one his father meant.
screen: `TWENTY RUPEES IN HIS HAND.` → `GO MAKE A GOOD DEAL.` → `NOT THE DEAL HIS FATHER MEANT.`

segments.voice: On the way, the story says, Nanak came across a group of holy men sitting by the road. Wandering ascetics, thin, quiet. He stopped and talked with them and found out they hadn't eaten in days. He looked at the twenty rupees. He thought about his father's words: make a good deal, a true one. And he went into the town and spent every coin on flour, lentils, butter and other food, brought it back and fed them all. Then he walked home with empty hands. Sacha sauda. Sacha means true. Sauda means a deal, a trade, a bargain. The true bargain. Nanak's answer to his father's instruction was that feeding the hungry was the truest deal there was. You didn't lose twenty rupees; you traded them for something that doesn't run out. His father didn't see it that way. The janamsakhis say Mehta Kalu was furious, and some tellings say he struck his son. Others in the family, and Rai Bular, stepped in to calm him. It's an honest touch in the story: the Guru's family didn't always understand him, and it hurt. Sikhs often see in this moment an early seed of the langar you met on day two: food for anyone hungry, bought with honest money, given freely. And there's a gurdwara today called Sacha Sauda, in Pakistan, on the spot where tradition says the holy men were fed. Nanak didn't disobey his father's words. He obeyed them more deeply than his father intended. Make a true deal, the father said. So he did.
screen: `HOLY MEN WHO HADN'T EATEN IN DAYS.` · `SACHA — TRUE. SAUDA — A DEAL.` · `A FATHER WHO DIDN'T UNDERSTAND.` · `AN EARLY SEED OF THE LANGAR.` · then, large: `THE TRUE BARGAIN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and think without guilt about where your money went this week: coffee, rent, something online. Now imagine holding twenty dollars, just as Nanak held twenty rupees, and picture someone who's hungry: a stranger on your street, a neighbor who's struggling, a food bank shelf. Picture that twenty turning into a meal in their hands, and sit with how that deal feels.
Sacha sauda. The true bargain: twenty rupees traded for a meal for the hungry, the best deal Nanak could make.
Your line: the best bargain. He walked home with empty hands. Until tomorrow.

27.title: The storehouse at Sultanpur
27.hook: weighing out grain as a storekeeper, he reaches thirteen, tera, which also means yours, and keeps saying it
27.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the tera story as a sakhi of Guru Nanak's years in Sultanpur Lodhi, and pilgrims visit the gurdwara there where tradition says the storehouse stood.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacha sauda, twenty rupees traded for a meal. The best bargain. Today, a steady job, and a strange way of counting.

Sultanpur. A young man stands in the government storehouse, in charge of the governor's grain. It comes in as taxes and goes out as wages and supplies, and the governor, Daulat Khan Lodi, wants someone honest running it. His sister's husband, Jai Ram, found him the job: steady, respectable, the kind his father hoped for. Tradition says Nanak is good at it, and honest. He has a family of his own now, and for a while it looks as if Mehta Kalu's son has settled down. Then comes the day he starts counting.
screen: `A STEADY JOB IN SULTANPUR.` → `THE GOVERNOR'S STOREHOUSE.` → `THEN HE STARTED COUNTING.`

segments.voice: The storehouse was the modikhana, and a storekeeper measured grain the old way: a scoop, a scale, counting aloud as each measure went into a customer's bag. Ik, do, tin: one, two, three. One day, the story says, Nanak counted up through ten, eleven, twelve, and reached thirteen. In Punjabi, thirteen is terah. Said aloud, it sounds just like tera, the word for yours. As in: yours, God. All of it, yours. And he stopped counting. Scoop after scoop went into the bag, and every one was tera. Tera. Tera. It sounds like a man losing his mind at work. But look at what it says. The grain, the scale, his own hands, the job: none of it was really his. So what was there to count? Of course someone complained to the governor that the storekeeper was giving the grain away. The accounts were checked, and the story says every grain was accounted for; some tellings even add a surplus. In Sultanpur today a gurdwara stands where tradition says the storehouse was, and weights said to be the ones he used are kept there. Tera isn't a trick with numbers. It's a way of holding everything with open hands: my money, my house, my time become yours, lent to me for a while. And a person who really believes that tends to measure generously.
screen: `THE MODIKHANA — THE GRAIN STORE.` · `IK, DO, TIN... UP TO THIRTEEN.` · `TERA — THIRTEEN, AND YOURS.` · `THE ACCOUNTS CAME OUT RIGHT.` · then, large: `TERA, TERA, ALL YOURS.`

segments.voice: Count slowly to twelve, one number on each breath out. On thirteen, let the number become tera, yours, and loosen your grip on whatever you're holding today. Then keep breathing, tera on each breath out.
Modikhana. The government storehouse at Sultanpur, where Nanak weighed out grain and counted to tera: thirteen, and yours.
Your line: tera, tera, all yours. Open hands, and an honest scale, every measure. Day twenty-seven, done.

28.title: Three days in the river
28.hook: he walks into the river Bein to bathe and is not seen for three days
28.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Bein river as the place where Guru Nanak's mission began; pilgrims visit Gurdwara Ber Sahib in Sultanpur Lodhi and some bathe in the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the modikhana, where the counting stopped at thirteen. Tera, tera, all yours. Today, the week's story turns.

Before dawn in Sultanpur. As he does every morning, the storekeeper walks down to the small river at the edge of town, the Bein, to bathe before the day begins. A servant waits on the bank with his clothes. Nanak steps into the water, goes under, and doesn't come up. The servant waits. Shouts. Runs for help. People come with ropes and nets; the governor himself, the story says, has the river searched. No body, no clothes, no trace. By evening the town has decided he's drowned. His sister grieves. A day passes. Then another.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, THE RIVER BEIN.` → `HE GOES UNDER.` → `AND DOESN'T COME UP.`

segments.voice: First, plainly: nobody knows what happened in those three days. No hymn of Nanak's tells it. What there is comes from the janamsakhis, and Sikhs treasure it. They say he was taken into the presence of God and given a cup of amrit, the nectar of immortality, and he drank it. He was sent back with a charge: go into the world, remember the Name, and teach others to remember it. On the third morning he walked out of the river. Some tellings link this moment with the root verse from days ten and eleven; not every telling does. Sikh tradition remembers the river as the place Nanak's mission began. What it was like from the inside, the sources leave in the water. Look at the week that led here: a baby born in Talwandi, a sister who saw first, a boy asking what the letters meant, a cobra's shade, a true bargain, a storekeeper saying tera. All of it building, quietly, until one morning he walked into a river and came out someone the whole town would have to reckon with. A gurdwara called Ber Sahib stands on the riverbank today, and tradition says the jujube tree there, the ber, is the one Nanak sat under.
